title: Challenge: Priority Scheduling

writing.exampleCaption: Complete std-only priority-scheduling program for its typed teaching fixture. Parsing and output construction are separate from the core algorithm.
writing.explanation:
Shortest duration, then smallest job ID. The worked program demonstrates this invariant on an independent fixture, so you can study the implementation before predicting the challenge result.

For teaching input `(id0,t0,d2),(id1,t0,d1),(id2,t3,d1)`, the worked program returns `1,0,2`. Its functions are complete and use only std. Adapt the same state transitions to the visible challenge input `(id0,t0,d3),(id1,t1,d1),(id2,t1,d2)`; predict that result before opening the answer reveal. The precise contract is: Parse unique job IDs with arrival t and positive duration d. Run the shortest available job nonpreemptively, breaking equal durations by smaller ID. Return completion order.

Return canonical output: lowercase booleans, decimal integers without leading zeros, comma-separated values and semicolon-separated groups, with no extra whitespace or final newline. Whole medians use integer form and half medians use .5. Textual sentinels such as none and # retain their stated meaning. String and character-grid fixtures use ASCII unless the lesson explicitly specifies Unicode scalar values.

Solve the exact task, not just the visible example: Parse unique job IDs with arrival t and positive duration d. Run the shortest available job nonpreemptively, breaking equal durations by smaller ID. Return completion order. On input `(id0,t0,d3),(id1,t1,d1),(id2,t1,d2)`, predict the output before opening the answer reveal. The revealed output is a test oracle for this case, while private checks exercise other legal cases. Start by stating the input grammar and output format in your own words. Parse the complete input, including surrounding whitespace, before relying on any convenient positions in the example.

Build the solution around one maintained claim: Order available work by the decision criterion while time controls when work becomes eligible. Decide what state represents that claim, how it is initialized, what a single update does, and when the algorithm stops. A heap keeps the current extremum accessible while new items arrive. Explain what belongs in the heap and what may be discarded. Trace the visible input by hand and record at least two intermediate states, not only the final answer. If the trace cannot justify your predicted output, there is a gap between the idea and the implementation.

Check both correctness and cost. The intended bound is O(n log n) time · O(n) space; explain which operation dominates it and how many times the input can trigger that operation. Check an empty stream, k equal to zero or to the input length, duplicate priorities, and stale entries if deletion is lazy. Add one small case that should succeed, one boundary case, and one case chosen to challenge the invariant. Compare your hand result with the program's result, then use a failing case to fix the earliest incorrect state transition rather than patching the final output.
writing.feedback: For this input the result is `0,1,2`. Shortest duration, then smallest job ID. Compare this independent fixture with the worked trace: At time 0 only job 0 with duration 3 is available, so it finishes first. At time 3 jobs 1 and 2 are ready; duration 1 beats duration 2. The completion order is 0,1,2; jobs are never interrupted mid-run.
